# Udayajātaka (Ja 458)

**ID:** Ja 458
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Prince Udayabhadda

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Udayajātaka* (Ja 458), translated as *Prince Udayabhadda*, is a narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. In the commentarial frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha relates the tale while dwelling at Jetavana to admonish a monk who has backslidden due to sensual desires [Fausböll 1887; SuttaCentral]. In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), Prince Udayabhadda and Princess Udayabhaddā are born to the same king by different mothers after descending from the Brahma realm [Fausböll 1887; Sujato 2011]. When their royal parents seek a suitable consort by fashioning an exquisite golden statue, only the princess matches its beauty, leading the half-siblings to wed [Fausböll 1887; Silk 2009; Sujato 2011]. Ruling the prosperous city of Surundha, the couple maintain a life of absolute celibacy (*brahmacariya*) in a shared chamber for seven hundred years without succumbing to lust [Fausböll 1887; SuttaCentral; Silk 2009]. After dying first, the Bodhisatta is reborn as Sakka; he subsequently tests the queen's virtue, teaches her the Dhamma, and inspires her to renounce the world as an ascetic, where upon death she is reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven [Fausböll 1887]. At the conclusion of the sermon, the backsliding monk attains stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) [Fausböll 1887].

Scholars note that the narrative pattern—a celibate marriage between an exceptionally beautiful couple matched by a golden statue—mirrors other Buddhist accounts, most notably the story of Mahākassapa and Bhaddā Kāpilānī [Silk 2009; Sujato 2011]. SuttaCentral identifies passage-level parallels in the *Bhītāsutta* of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (SN 1.75) and two Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* parallels (SA 1315 and SA2 314), noting also a citation in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus independently confirms Pali-internal reuse with SN 1 and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, while computing cross-language matches with the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (scoring up to 95) and parallel segments in Chinese and Tibetan collections [DharmaNexus]. Beyond the Pali tradition, the narrative was adapted into Sanskrit kavya in the *Haribhaṭṭajātakamālā* (*Udayajātaka*) [Martin 2006], and early visual depictions of the story are preserved among the Hinayana wall paintings of Cave 9 at Ajanta [Spink 2006].
